intro: Each persona is composite, illustrative, and grounded in the Marblehead market and ACS distributions. They are not real residents. Numbers use FY26 base tax rate ($8.56 per $1,000), the proposed tier 3 override ($1.50 per $1,000), and current local insurance/utility estimates.

personas.name: Eleanor
personas.tag: 78, widow, lives alone on Social Security
personas.story: Bought a 1,200 sq ft Cape with her husband in 1972 for $35,000. Mortgage paid off in 1998. Husband died in 2009; she has lived alone since.
personas.relief_eligible: Clause 41C borderline (income at the local limit). Circuit Breaker yes.
personas.if_claimed: If she claims Circuit Breaker and 41C, total relief could be ~$2,000/yr, dropping her current bill to about $2,965 (housing burden 30.4%). The override still adds $870 on top — credits cut the base bill, not the override increment.
personas.key_point: Low fixed income, paid-off small home — but 'paid off' doesn't mean cheap. The tax bill alone is 22.6% of her income.

personas.name: Bob and Carol
personas.tag: 72 and 71, retired couple, paid-off mid-range home
personas.story: Bob retired from his manufacturing job in 2018. Carol retired from teaching in 2019. Pension plus Social Security plus a small annual Required Minimum Distribution covers their expenses.
personas.relief_eligible: 41C: no (over income). 17D: yes (both 70+). Circuit Breaker: yes.
personas.if_claimed: 17D credit ~$175. Circuit Breaker credit ~$2,000. Total reduction ~$2,175. Net current bill ~$5,700. Override still adds $1,380.
personas.key_point: Not cost-burdened by the 30% rule, but the override is a real $115/month line item for a fixed-income couple. They feel the squeeze even though ACS doesn't classify them as cost-burdened.

personas.name: Margaret
personas.story: Sold her medical practice in 2020. Took Social Security at 67. Lives off a $1.5M portfolio: about $34K shows on her tax return as SS and small dividends, plus $80K/yr from selling appreciated stock. ACS counts only the $34K.
personas.relief_eligible: 41C: no (over income limit even on ACS-reported income). Circuit Breaker: borderline.
personas.if_claimed: Realistically none. Her actual situation is comfortable; the cost-burden classification is an ACS measurement artifact.
personas.key_point: Counts as 'severely cost-burdened' in the ACS data but is not actually distressed. Some unknown share of the 903 cost-burdened seniors falls into this category.

personas.name: James and Sarah
personas.story: James works as a mechanic. Sarah left her bookkeeping job in 2022 to care full-time for her mother, who has Alzheimer's and lives with them. Their teenage daughter is in high school.
personas.relief_eligible: Nothing. Too young for senior clauses. Not a veteran. No qualifying disability.
personas.if_claimed: No path. The under-65 cost-burden ceiling doesn't apply, but the override hits in full.
personas.key_point: The under-65 'missing middle.' Under any cost-burden definition they're fine — but they have no relief mechanism at all if their situation changes.

personas.name: David
personas.story: Wife died two years ago after a long illness. He lost her Social Security benefit. He kept the house they bought together in 1989 because moving feels like leaving her behind.
personas.relief_eligible: 41C: possibly (income at threshold). 17D: complex (he was widowed at 69, not 70+ when his wife died). Circuit Breaker: yes.
personas.if_claimed: Circuit Breaker alone could reduce his bill by ~$2,500. The Social Security loss is the real shock; the override compounds it modestly.
personas.key_point: The override is not what makes his situation hard. The loss of his wife's Social Security benefit was. The override adds $90/month on top.

personas.name: Anand and Priya (the Patels)
personas.tag: 36 and 34, two kids, recent home purchase
personas.story: Both engineers. Moved to Marblehead in 2022 for the schools. Bought their home at near-peak prices with a 6.8% mortgage. Two kids in elementary school.
personas.home_str: $1,050,000 purchased 2022, current value similar; $4,800/month mortgage P+I
personas.key_point: High income, high cost burden, no relief eligibility. They chose to stretch for the schools. The override is meaningful but doesn't change the fundamental decision they already made.

personas.name: Tom
personas.story: Divorced in 2018. Bought a 2BR condo for $385K in 2019. Has primary custody of his 14-year-old. Works in commercial real estate; income is variable but averaged around $58K the past three years.
personas.key_point: Single parent, modest income, no relief eligibility. Already at 58.8% housing burden. The override adds 1.3 percentage points.

personas.name: Linda and Mark
personas.story: Both work professional jobs. One child in high school. Bought their home in 2010 with a 30-year mortgage; about 17 years remaining. Refinanced twice for lower rates.
personas.key_point: Standard middle-class Marblehead family. Cost-burdened by the ACS rule because they still have a mortgage. The override is a $118/month line item — meaningful, not transformative.

personas.name: Bill and Jennifer Williamson
personas.tag: 56 and 54, established, two kids in college
personas.story: Bill is a partner at a Boston law firm; Jennifer is a senior product manager. Two kids at private colleges. Mortgage paid off in 2021. They have substantial savings and retirement accounts.
personas.relief_eligible: None — but they don't need it.
personas.key_point: Highest dollar override impact in this set ($181/month), smallest burden in income terms (0.7 percentage point increase). When override proponents say 'most households can absorb this,' households like the Williamsons are who they have in mind. For them, $181/month is real but unremarkable.

personas.name: Sasha and Mike
personas.tag: 41 and 42, two-professional couple, new high-end home
personas.story: Both work in tech. Two kids. Moved from a smaller home in 2024 to a larger one because they wanted the schools and the space. New mortgage at 6.5%.
personas.key_point: High-income but high-leverage. They count as cost-burdened in ACS data but they chose this stretch. They're roughly 7% of the cost-burdened cohort: high-income households who bought above their comfort range.
